global.headline: TRUMP THREATENS TO DECLARE HORMUZ A "TERRITORY OF THE UNITED STATES" AS IRAN HITS TWO MORE UAE TANKERS
summary: At a rally at a police academy in Garden City, New York, Trump said "after we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States." It was unclear how seriously the remark was intended, or how Washington would assert territorial claims over a waterway bordered and shared by Iran and Oman, over which the US has no jurisdiction. Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi dismissed it, saying Tehran would not be intimidated and that the strait would only open or close under Iran's own authority.

The same day, the UAE said two tankers belonging to state-owned operator ADNOC were targeted by Iranian drones while transiting Hormuz, calling the attacks "acts of piracy" and a breach of UN Security Council Resolution 2817; no casualties were reported. It is the third ADNOC vessel hit this week and the 15th since the war began, with the campaign's cumulative toll against ADNOC's fleet now standing at one crew member killed and 20 injured.
global.geopolitical: Trump's territorial claim over an international strait he has no legal grounds to annex drew an immediate, dismissive rebuttal from Iran, but paired with a second UAE tanker attack in a week it signals Washington's rhetoric is shifting from blockade-enforcement to outright assertions of control even as Gulf partners like the UAE keep absorbing the costs of Iran's continued strikes on commercial shipping.
global.socioeconomic: A fifteenth attack on ADNOC's own fleet is a reminder that six months into the war, commercial shipping — not just military assets — continues to bear its costs, keeping Gulf insurance and freight premiums elevated even as Brent crude has eased back from its late-July peak.

global.headline: COLOMBIA EARTHQUAKE TOLL RISES TO 285 AS PEREIRA RESCUERS RACE A TRAPPED VENDOR, AND MEXICO'S REJECTED RESCUE TEAM IS QUIETLY LET IN AFTER ALL
summary: Colombia's National Disaster Risk Management Unit put Friday's confirmed earthquake death toll at 285, up from Thursday's 265, with more than 3,500 injured and roughly 379 still missing as the toll reconciliation continues. In Pereira, rescuers using vibration-detection equipment worked through the night around street vendor Pablo Loaiza, buried since Monday's 7.4-magnitude quake beneath a collapsed bakery; family members said Loaiza appeared to respond when rescuers asked him to knock from beneath the rubble, but his fate remained unresolved as the operation shifted from rescue toward recovery.

Days after Bogotá said it would request foreign rescue teams from only four countries and Mexico's government said its Topos Azteca brigade's offer had been turned down, the 45-member Mexican team — which had been in Venezuela for 41 days after that country's own earthquakes — was in fact allowed into Colombia and carried out its first rescue in Cali, digging a dog out of collapsed debris. No official explanation was given for the reversal.
global.geopolitical: Colombia quietly admitting the very Mexican rescue brigade it had publicly turned away, without ever acknowledging the reversal, undercuts the government's own account of the earlier snub and adds another episode of administrative confusion to a five-week-old administration's handling of its first major disaster.
global.socioeconomic: With the toll still climbing and the search shifting to recovery, the scale of the rebuilding task ahead — thousands of destroyed homes across Chocó and Valle del Cauca — is starting to eclipse the search-and-rescue story as the earthquake's defining long-term cost.

global.headline: ZAMBIA SUSPENDS PRESIDENTIAL VOTE COUNT OVER VIOLENCE AGAINST POLL STAFF AND BALLOT THEFT
summary: The Electoral Commission of Zambia suspended vote counting nationwide on Friday, a day after presidential and parliamentary elections, citing attacks on polling officials and the theft of marked ballot papers from ballot boxes at some stations. The commission's chief electoral officer said the violence was targeted at poll staff specifically and that it would review the suspension within 24 hours.

Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, a first-time presidential candidate, claimed victory and said the delay created "an opportunity for interference with or manipulation of the results," alleging soldiers had taken control of vote-counting stations in at least one town and that ballot boxes had been removed from others. President Hakainde Hichilema, seeking a second term, had been widely seen as the favourite heading into polling day.
global.geopolitical: A vote-count suspension over violence and alleged ballot theft is a serious credibility test for one of southern Africa's more stable multiparty democracies, and the dueling claims of manipulation from a sitting president's team and a first-time opposition challenger raise the risk of a contested outcome regardless of who the count ultimately favours.
global.socioeconomic: Zambia is Africa's second-largest copper producer, and prolonged post-election uncertainty risks unsettling investment in a mining sector already central to the country's debt-restructuring and growth plans under Hichilema's government.

global.headline: UKRAINE HITS RUSSIA'S BALTIC OIL PORT UST-LUGA WITH 54 DRONES, SIXTH STRIKE THIS YEAR
summary: Ukraine's military struck the Ust-Luga oil terminal in Russia's Leningrad Oblast overnight with 54 drones, damaging two processing plants and sparking a fire, Ukraine's General Staff said. Regional governor Alexander Drozdenko said air defences shot down 51 of the drones, that a blaze at the port was extinguished by morning and that no one was hurt.

It is at least the sixth Ukrainian strike on Ust-Luga this year — one of Russia's largest Baltic Sea export terminals for crude oil and petroleum products — underscoring Kyiv's sustained campaign against Russian oil-export infrastructure, which two days earlier also hit grain terminals and naval vessels at the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.
global.geopolitical: A sixth strike this year on a single major export terminal shows Ukraine can now repeatedly reach deep into Russia's Baltic infrastructure despite Russian air defences, widening its economic-pressure campaign geographically beyond the Black Sea assets it has more routinely targeted.
global.socioeconomic: Repeated disruption to Ust-Luga's oil-export capacity adds to the cumulative strain on Russia's energy revenues from the Novorossiysk and refinery strikes already tracked this year, even as any single incident's damage is patched over within days.

global.headline: WEST BANK SIEGE OF PALESTINIAN HOMES ENTERS SIXTH DAY AS AMNESTY, UN CONDEMN ISRAEL OVER QUSRA
summary: The siege of Palestinian homes in the West Bank village of Qusra, near Nablus, entered its sixth day on Friday. Amnesty International called it a "relentless escalation" in a well-documented pattern of coordinated, state-backed settler violence aimed at displacing Palestinians, while the Washington Post reported that Israeli troops largely stood by as settlers blockaded the homes, cutting water and electricity, even as the military says its own deployment — which has pushed roughly 20 Palestinian families out of their homes and converted several properties into military positions — is meant to prevent clashes.

The development extends Thursday's story, in which Israeli forces dismantled two settler outposts and US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, a longtime supporter of the settler movement, called the siege "an act of terror." Residents say the pattern has repeated for days: forces periodically clear settlers from the site, only for them to return and re-establish their positions once the troops withdraw.
global.geopolitical: Formal condemnation from Amnesty International and the UN, layered on top of a pro-settler US ambassador's own "act of terror" language, is building unusually broad and unusual-source pressure on Israel over a single village siege, even as reporting that troops stood by while it happened undercuts the state's own framing of its role as protective.
global.socioeconomic: A week of cut water and power aimed at three families is a small-scale illustration of the broader displacement pattern the UN has already flagged this year — more than 1,430 settler-violence incidents and roughly 3,800 Palestinians displaced — in which sustained pressure on daily life, not formal eviction, does the work of pushing residents out.

singapore.headline: LAW MINISTER URGES LAW SOCIETY TO RELEASE AUDIT REPORT ON "SIGNIFICANT FAILINGS" AFTER TENSE CLOSED-DOOR MEMBERS' MEETING
summary: A closed-door dialogue session the Law Society held for its members on Wednesday saw raised voices and calls for the full release of an independent audit that found significant failings in leadership, workplace culture and governance at the Society between 2022 and 2025 — a report Law Minister Edwin Tong first disclosed in a 5 August parliamentary reply, which found no deliberate financial impropriety or intentional cover-up. More than 200 members had earlier petitioned for greater transparency over the findings.

In a statement on Thursday, Tong said the audit committee's report raises "significant issues" about the Law Society's workplace culture and its own proper functioning, and urged the Society to share the underlying reports with members, with appropriate redactions.
singapore.socioeconomic: The transparency standoff pits the Law Society's institutional instinct for confidentiality against mounting member pressure for accountability, arriving the same week its own disciplinary bench struck off Opposition Leader Pritam Singh — testing whether the body will apply to itself the openness it demands of others.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE SCAM VICTIMS LOSE $15.1M IN A SINGLE CRYPTO JOB-INTERVIEW BREACH, $6.1M MORE TO ICA/CHINA-OFFICIAL IMPERSONATION
summary: The police and Cyber Security Agency said Thursday that scammers posing as a cryptocurrency recruiter on LinkedIn lured an employee through fake video interviews (with the "interviewer's" camera disabled throughout) and a rigged take-home coding assessment that installed malware on a company device. Attackers used the resulting foothold to steal a session token, bypass multi-factor authentication, access the company's code repository and ultimately push through crypto transfers totalling S$15.1 million (US$11.8 million) — one of the largest single-incident scam losses reported here this year.

Separately, police said scammers impersonating Immigration and Checkpoints Authority officers, who then hand victims to a second scammer posing as a Chinese official demanding money for "investigation or bail," have caused at least S$6.1 million in losses across 72 reported cases since January.
singapore.socioeconomic: A single breach draining S$15.1 million by compromising a company's own security controls, not just an individual's judgment, signals scam syndicates increasingly targeting corporate systems directly — even as authorities' own earlier 2026 interventions, which blocked a combined S$7 million or so in separate operations with crypto exchanges, show enforcement still running behind the losses.

singapore.headline: ABOUT 70 SINGAPORE PRESCHOOLS CLOSED EACH YEAR FROM 2023 TO 2025 AS ENROLMENT SLIDES
summary: An average of about 70 preschools closed in Singapore each year between 2023 and 2025, the large majority of them private centres without government support; roughly half of the centres that closed in 2025 had been operating below 40 per cent of their enrolment capacity beforehand.

The closures are being driven by falling birth rates shrinking the pool of children, rising operating costs and manpower shortages, and a shift in family preference toward more affordable, government-supported preschool options — leaving smaller private operators the most exposed to the sector's structural squeeze.
singapore.socioeconomic: The closures are a concrete, sector-level expression of Singapore's broader demographic strain — a record-low total fertility rate and 2025 births falling below 30,000 for the first time since independence — showing how a shrinking birth cohort is already reshaping the market for early-childhood care even as government-backed alternatives absorb the families that remain.

word.definition: Excessive pride or self-confidence, especially arrogance that disregards natural, legal or practical limits and typically precipitates a downfall.
word.etymology: From Ancient Greek ὕβρις (hybris), originally denoting outrageous, norm-violating conduct in Greek tragedy — where a hero's hubris routinely draws down nemesis, the retribution that follows; entered English via classical scholarship in the 19th century.
word.example: Trump's vow to "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz — an international waterway the US has no jurisdiction over — a "territory of the United States" was met with a shrug from Iran, whose deputy foreign minister said the strait would open or close on Tehran's authority alone, not Washington's.
